prompt: Match each question to the test that fits it.
hint: Outcome type, then number and kind of groups.

pairs.left: Is the filling machine's mean 1000 g?
Do the same ten couriers get faster after a course?
Do four neighbourhoods differ in delivery time?
Does the new page convert a larger share of visitors?

prompt: Horta compares the share of pix payments in two neighbourhoods. What kind of test fits?
hint: Is the outcome a number or a category?

choices.text: A t test on the payment codes
choices.why: Payment is categorical; averaging its codes is lesson 2's mistake.

choices.text: Chi-square on the counts
choices.why: Right. A categorical outcome in two groups is a table of counts.

choices.text: ANOVA, since there are categories
choices.why: ANOVA compares means of a numerical outcome across groups.

choices.text: A paired t test
choices.why: Nothing is measured twice on the same units.

prompt: For the ten couriers, the differences after minus before have mean −1.21 and standard deviation 1.65. What is the paired t statistic? Give two decimal places.
The training data gave p = 0.35 analysed as two separate groups and p = 0.046 analysed as pairs. Why so different?
hint: How much do couriers differ from each other?

choices.text: The paired test is more lenient and should be avoided
choices.why: It is the right test for this design, not a lenient one.

choices.text: The two analyses used different data
choices.why: They used the same twenty numbers.

choices.text: Ten is too few for a two-group test
choices.why: Ten is small for either; the design is the difference.

choices.text: Pairing strips out how couriers differ
choices.why: Right. Each courier is compared with themselves, so only the change is left.

prompt: Why is Welch's version the safe default for comparing two separate groups?

choices.text: It does not assume equal spreads
choices.why: Right. When spreads are equal it agrees closely with the older test; when they differ it is still right.

choices.text: It always gives a smaller p-value
choices.why: Not so; it gives the honest p-value for unequal spreads.

choices.text: It needs no assumptions at all
choices.why: It still assumes independence and roughly normal means.

choices.text: It works on ranks instead of values
choices.why: That is the Mann-Whitney test.

prompt: In a table with row total 2,000, column total 482 and grand total 4,000, what is the expected count in that cell?
hint: Row total × column total ÷ grand total.

prompt: The checkout test gave χ² = 4.16 with 1 degree of freedom and p = 0.041. What is the right reading?

choices.text: The new page converts 4.16 times better
choices.why: χ² is a test statistic, not a ratio of rates; the rates are 11.0% and 13.1%.

choices.text: There is a 4.1% chance the pages are the same
choices.why: That is the familiar misreading of a p-value.

choices.text: Probably more than chance alone
choices.why: Right. At 5%, the null of equal rates is rejected, though not by a wide margin.

choices.text: The table is too small for the test
choices.why: Every expected count is far above 5.

prompt: Why should lesson 1's table of twelve orders by neighbourhood and payment not be tested with chi-square?

choices.text: Payment is not categorical
choices.why: It is categorical; the problem is size.

choices.text: Chi-square needs exactly two rows
choices.why: It works for any number of rows and columns.

choices.text: Its expected counts are far below 5
choices.why: Right. With twelve orders in twelve cells, the approximation fails; Fisher's exact test or more data is needed.

choices.text: The neighbourhoods are not independent of each other
choices.why: Independence concerns the orders, and nothing suggests they are linked.

prompt: Why use ANOVA instead of six t tests to compare four neighbourhoods?

choices.text: Six tests raise the false-alarm rate; one test does not
choices.why: Right. Lesson 14: many tests at 5% each make a false alarm much more likely.

choices.text: ANOVA is more precise about which pair differs
choices.why: It says only that at least one differs, not which.

choices.text: t tests cannot compare neighbourhoods
choices.why: They can compare any two; the problem is running many.

choices.text: ANOVA needs no assumptions
choices.why: It assumes independence, roughly normal means and similar spreads.

prompt: An ANOVA has a between-group mean square of 3,399.1 and a within-group mean square of 25.7. What is F? Give one decimal place.
An ANOVA on four groups rejects the null. What does that tell you?

choices.text: All four group means differ from each other
choices.why: It says at least one differs, not that every pair does.

choices.text: The largest group mean is the one that differs
choices.why: It does not say which; follow-up comparisons do.

choices.text: The groups have different spreads
choices.why: ANOVA tests means; it assumes similar spreads.

choices.text: At least one differs, but not which
choices.why: Right. Tukey's honestly significant difference is the usual next step.

prompt: Why are rank-based tests less affected by an outlier?
hint: What does a rank keep, and what does it throw away?

choices.text: They delete the outliers first
choices.why: Nothing is deleted; the outlier just becomes the largest rank.

choices.text: An outlier is just the top rank
choices.why: Right. Ranks ignore distances, so extremeness beyond 'largest' does not count.

choices.text: They use the median instead of the data
choices.why: They use every value's rank, not one summary.

choices.text: They need larger samples
choices.why: If anything, they are most useful in small samples.

prompt: Match each test of means to its rank-based alternative.
A survey compares star ratings, 1 to 5, between two delivery services with 15 customers each. Which test suits it best?
hint: Ordinal outcome, small samples, two separate groups.

choices.text: Welch's t on the mean ratings
choices.why: Ratings are ordinal and the samples small; a mean rests on assumptions lesson 2 warned about.

choices.text: Mann-Whitney
choices.why: Right. It needs only the order of the ratings, and suits small samples.

choices.text: A paired t test
choices.why: The two groups are different customers, not the same ones twice.

choices.text: ANOVA
choices.why: With two groups ANOVA is a t test, with the same problems.

prompt: Which assumption shared by every test in this lesson can no formula check?
hint: Which one is about how the data was gathered?

choices.text: Normality
choices.why: Histograms and boxplots check the shape.

choices.text: Equal spreads
choices.why: Comparing the standard deviations checks that.

choices.text: Expected counts of at least 5
choices.why: Those are computed directly from the table.

choices.text: Independence of the observations
choices.why: Right. It depends on how the data was collected, which only thinking about the design can check.

prompt: Put the steps of testing a difference in the order this lesson recommends.
items: Look at the data by group
Think about whether the observations are independent
Choose the test from the outcome and the groups
Run it, and the alternative if an assumption is doubtful
